name: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
title: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
answer: Draft, Then a Person Edits is the most common pattern in the book: an AI tool produces a first version of a document and a person reads, corrects and decides whether it is used. It matters because the time saved is real but the draft is never finished work, and the adult who signs it remains the owner.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern describes AI as a fast assistant rather than an author. A tool writes a first version of a lesson plan, a parent letter, practice questions, a rubric, a summary of an individualized education program for a parent, or a grant narrative, and a person then reads it, fixes it and decides whether it goes out. It solves the problem of the blank page, since the tool supplies a starting point and the adult supplies the judgment. The person who signs the document owns it, whatever the tool contributed.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The pattern looks different by grade band. In a preschool classroom a teacher might ask an approved tool to draft the weekly note home, then add the class news that only she knows. In a middle school a science teacher might request three versions of the same reading at different levels, then check that the science stayed correct in all three. In a high school a counselor might draft a plain language explanation of graduation requirements for families. Figure 2.3 sets out four steps that make the pattern safe, and the checking gets stricter as the stakes rise.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this pattern with research support. In one study, 15 teachers in five English primary schools used AI for lesson planning over two terms and reported that their weekly planning time fell from about 10 hours to under 5 (Carson et al., 2026). The same teachers said the saved time was often swallowed by other demands, so the hours never turned into anything a principal could see. A second study found that when researchers asked a chatbot to write a first grade science lesson, the result was well organized and followed a familiar teaching model, but it included questionable steps, left out details, and listed a teaching resource that did not exist (Powell & Courchesne, 2024). A teacher who skimmed it would have handed a fake source to a room full of six year olds.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The draft needs real editing, not a quick glance, because the first grade science example shows how a plausible looking lesson can contain a resource that does not exist. For anything touching a student's services, grades, or records, the names come out before the text goes in, and the final version is checked against the real file. That rule is easy to state and easy to skip, which is why it appears in every chapter that uses this pattern. The decision about whether a document goes out stays with the person who signs it, and the time a tool saves can disappear into other demands unless it is protected.
